newsitem.title: USA: Dollar scores vs mark, retreats vs yen at US noon. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dollar scores vs mark, retreats vs yen at US noon. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]

text.p: The dollar powered to another 71-month high versus the mark but faltered against the yen as cross-trading dominated activity ahead of a key speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, dealers said.

Mark/yen drew much of the focus, extending its slide to over a yen from last night's highs (corrects from lows). Speculators reportedly went short the yen overnight only to pay a heavy price as the Japanese unit roared higher, traders said.
"Some very big positions were put on against the yen and those guys are sucking wind right now," said one trader at a U.S. bank.
Dollar/mark's surprising overnight rally caught a second wind by late morning as shorts threw in the towel and stops were triggered as the greenback neared 1.82, dealers said.
"Dollar/mark has a chance to trade higher, but it seems like the New York market walked in and was a little bit stunned by the overnight ranges, said John Beerling, chief dealer at Norwest Bank.

The dollar at midday stood at 1.8168/78 marks, up from 1.8130/40 at the open and 1.7960/70 at Monday's close. Just before noon the greenback peaked at 1.8197. Dollar/yen fell to 115.50/55 from 116.00/10.
Mark/yen stood near 63.50, off from an overnight peak at 64.70. Dealers cited continuing flight to the yen from southeast Asian players in the wake of recent heavy selling of exotic Asian currencies.

"The Japanese came back from holiday and the Philippine peso was under pressure again today. The yen is like the pound in Europe, it gets a lot of support in times of stress," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group.
The yen also gained on the Australian dollar and sterling, dealers said. Meanwhile a knock-out option at dollar/yen 116.50 expired during U.S. morning, bringing fresh yen buying.
"At this level, there are a lot of people looking to sell dollar/yen. It got a little too long yesterday," said a trader at an Australian bank in New York.
But dollar/mark continued to find ample buyers following the latest official indications that Europe's proposed single currency will be softer than the mark, dealers said.

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick got most of the attention, telling German radio the euro could be stable even if Germany posts a deficit of 3.2 percent of GDP and France of 3.3 percent.
The tacit acknowledgement that the EU will allow nations to violate the 3.0-percent budget deficit-to-GDP ratio continues to hammer the mark, dealers said.

"We are seeing a quiet acquiescence to a deutschemark devaluation," said Malpede. "As long as they don't have notable imported inflation, the Germans will continue to try to compete (in global markets) with a weaker deutschemark."
Yet other players remained on the alert for signs of Bundesbank intervention, claiming the central bank's leaders would act to stop the dollar's advance if they believed they could.
"People are viewing the Bundesbank's silence as a commitment to a higher dollar, a weak euro and a weak mark. But that's not necessarily true," said the U.S. bank trader.
"The only way they could fight the trend is with higher interest rates or faster (German) growth and on both of which they have no flexibility right now," she added.
In other trade, the dollar slipped to 1.4810/20 Swiss francs from 1.4852/62. Sterling fell to $1.6730/40 from $1.6760/70. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3814/19 from C$1.3796/01.
